title: PAROXYSMAL EXTREME PAIN DISORDER
alt_titles: PAIN, SUBMANDIBULAR, OCULAR, AND RECTAL, WITH FLUSHING

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that paroxysmal extreme pain disorder (PEXPD) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the SCN9A gene, which encodes the voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.7.

checks.explanation: The abstract says SCN9A encodes Nav1.7, and calling Nav1.7 a voltage-gated sodium channel is standard nomenclature.

paragraphs.text: Paroxysmal extreme pain disorder (PEPD), previously known as familial rectal pain, is an inherited condition with paroxysms of rectal, ocular, or submandibular pain with flushing (Fertleman et al., 2006). Onset is in the neonatal period or infancy and the disorder persists throughout life. Autonomic manifestations, including skin flushing, harlequin color change, tonic attacks, and syncope with bradycardia, predominate at first. Later, attacks of excruciating deep burning pain occur, triggered by factors such as defecation, cold wind, eating, and emotion (Fertleman et al., 2007).

paragraphs.text: Hayden and Grossman (1959) described the disorder as rectal, ocular, and submaxillary pain, a familial autonomic disorder related to proctalgia fugax. Dugan (1972) used the name familial rectal pain, and Mann and Cree (1972) also published on familial rectal pain. Fertleman and Ferrie (2006) proposed that familial rectal pain syndrome be renamed paroxysmal extreme pain disorder.

paragraphs.text: Fertleman et al. (2007) described the clinical phenotype in 77 individuals from 15 families identified by an international consortium; 14 affected individuals completed a validated pain questionnaire. The disorder began in the neonatal period or infancy and persisted throughout life. At first, autonomic manifestations predominated: all had skin flushing, and most had harlequin color change and tonic attacks. Dramatic syncopes with bradycardia and sometimes asystole were common. Later, the disorder was characterized by attacks of excruciating deep burning pain, often in the rectal, ocular, or jaw areas but also diffuse. Attacks were triggered by factors such as defecation, cold wind, eating, and emotion.

paragraphs.text: In 11 families and 2 sporadic cases with PEPD, Fertleman et al. (2006) identified 8 different missense mutations in the SCN9A gene. Functional analysis in vitro of 3 of the mutant Nav1.7 channels showed reduced fast inactivation, leading to persistent sodium current. By contrast, other SCN9A mutations that cause primary erythermalgia are associated with more negative activation thresholds. Carbamazepine, which is effective in PEPD but not in primary erythermalgia, selectively blocked the persistent current of PEPD mutants but did not affect the negative activation threshold of a primary erythermalgia mutant. Fertleman et al. (2006) concluded that PEPD and primary erythermalgia are allelic disorders with distinct underlying biophysical mechanisms.

paragraphs.text: In a 3-year-old girl with PEPD who had painful micturition, Meglič et al. (2014) identified a heterozygous c.554G-A mutation in the SCN9A gene, resulting in an arg185-to-his (R185H) substitution. She inherited the mutation from her father, who had occasional jaw pain. The authors noted that the same mutation had been found in patients with small fiber sensory neuropathy. They suggested that intra- and interfamilial phenotypic variability associated with gain-of-function Nav1.7 variants might explain this.
